nodes.label: The Abbasid Caliphate
nodes.full: Baghdad: the distant overlord of the caliphal province, which sent Muhammad ibn Ziyad to hold the Tihama and whose weakening let autonomous dynasties form.
nodes.src: background — al-Tabari; Kay, 'Yaman' (1892).

nodes.label: The Fatimid Caliphate
nodes.full: Cairo: the Ismaili caliphate whose missionary work created Sulayhid Yemen, whose 1130 schism Queen Arwa navigated, and whose fall in 1171 left Yemen the guardian of the Tayyibi daʿwa.
nodes.src: background — Daftary, 'The Ismailis' (2007).

nodes.label: Ayyubid & Mamluk Egypt
nodes.full: Saladin's realm and its Mamluk successor: the conqueror of Yemen in 1174, then for two and a half centuries its northern rival over Mecca, the Red Sea customs and the guardianship of the Holy Cities.
nodes.src: background — al-Maqrizi; Vallet, 'L'Arabie marchande' (2010).

nodes.label: The Indian Ocean world
nodes.full: India, the Karimi spice houses, the East African coast and Ming China: the trade that made Aden rich and the Rasulid state solvent.
nodes.src: background — Goitein and Friedman, 'India Traders of the Middle Ages' (2008).

nodes.label: Portugal
nodes.full: The new power in the Indian Ocean after 1498: its blockade of the Red Sea mouth and failed assault on Aden wrecked the Karimi economy and prompted the Mamluk expedition to Yemen.
nodes.src: background — Serjeant, 'The Portuguese off the South Arabian Coast' (1963).

nodes.label: The Ottomans
nodes.full: The conquerors of Egypt in 1517, who absorbed the stranded Mamluk force in Yemen and inherited a claim to the country.
nodes.src: background — added on review; al-Nahrawali, al-Barq al-Yamani.

nodes.label: Yemen accepts Islam, and the Ridda
nodes.full: The Persian governor Badhan and the Abna accepted Islam around 628; the prophet-claimant al-Aswad al-ʿAnsi briefly seized Sanaa and was killed in 632, and the Ridda wars then restored Muslim control. Yemen entered Islam early and, after one convulsion, permanently.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History I; Ibn Hisham, Sira; Madelung on the Islamisation of Yemen.

nodes.label: A province of the Caliphate
nodes.full: For two centuries Yemen was governed for Medina, then Damascus, then Baghdad — a recruiting ground for the conquest armies and a fiscal backwater, its politics dominated by tribal and sectarian revolt. The Great Mosque of Sanaa was founded in this period.
nodes.src: al-Tabari; al-Razi, Taʾrikh madinat Sanaa; Wilferd Madelung, 'The origins of the Yemenite Hijra'.

nodes.label: The Ziyadids of Zabid
nodes.full: The caliph al-Maʾmun sent Muhammad ibn Ziyad to pacify the Tihama; he founded the city of Zabid and a dynasty that ruled the coast in the Abbasids' name but effectively on its own for two centuries. Zabid grew into a centre of Sunni learning.
nodes.src: ʿUmara al-Yamani, Taʾrikh al-Yaman; Kay's translation, 'Yaman: Its Early Mediaeval History' (1892).

nodes.label: The Yuʿfirids of Sanaa
nodes.full: A highland dynasty claiming Himyarite descent, the Yuʿfirids held Sanaa and the central highlands, at times acknowledging Baghdad and at times fighting both the Ziyadids below and the new Zaydi imamate to the north.
nodes.src: ʿUmara al-Yamani; al-Hamdani, al-Iklil; Kay (1892).

nodes.label: Al-Hadi ila'l-Haqq founds the Zaydi imamate
nodes.full: Yahya ibn al-Husayn, a Husaynid sayyid from Medina, was invited to arbitrate among the tribes of Saʿda and stayed to found the Zaydi imamate and its Hadawi school of law. The institution he created governed the northern highlands until 1962.
nodes.src: al-Hadi's own works and the sira by ʿAli ibn Muhammad al-ʿAlawi; Madelung, 'Der Imam al-Qasim ibn Ibrahim' and the Zaydi studies.

nodes.label: The imams through the medieval centuries
nodes.full: Zaydi doctrine held that any qualified descendant of ʿAli and Fatima could claim the imamate by rising in arms (khuruj). The result was a discontinuous line — contracting to Saʿda, expanding to Sanaa, sometimes with rival claimants — but a continuous institution.
nodes.src: the Zaydi biographical literature (tabaqat); Cornelis van Arendonk, 'Les débuts de l'imamat zaidite au Yémen' (1960).

nodes.label: ʿAli al-Sulayhi unites Yemen for the Fatimids
nodes.full: ʿAli ibn Muhammad al-Sulayhi, an Ismaili chief from the Haraz mountains, brought most of Yemen under one rule as a vassal of the Fatimid caliph in Cairo. He was ambushed and killed by the Najahids in 1066 on his way to the pilgrimage.
nodes.src: ʿUmara al-Yamani, Taʾrikh al-Yaman; Husain al-Hamdani, 'The Sulayhid dynasty'; Farhad Daftary, 'The Ismailis' (2007).

nodes.label: Queen Arwa bint Ahmad
nodes.full: Arwa ruled Yemen for over fifty years from Jibla, first with her husbands and then alone — coining money and pronouncing the khutba in her own name, holding the Fatimid religious rank of hujja, and steering the Tayyibi succession that made Yemen the seat of that daʿwa.
nodes.src: ʿUmara al-Yamani; Leila al-Imad, 'Women and Religion in the Fatimid Caliphate: the case of al-Sayyida al-Hurra'; Daftary, 'The Ismailis'.

nodes.label: The Najahids and the coastal states
nodes.full: The Najahids of Zabid, founded by Ethiopian military slaves, fought the Sulayhids for the Tihama for over a century; around them spun the Zurayids of Aden, the Hamdanids of Sanaa and, finally, the Mahdids — a scatter of small states that the Ayyubids swept away.
nodes.src: ʿUmara al-Yamani, Taʾrikh al-Yaman; Kay (1892); G. Rex Smith on the pre-Ayyubid dynasties.

nodes.label: Turan Shah conquers Yemen for the Ayyubids
nodes.full: Saladin's brother Turan Shah overran the fragmented country in 1174; Ayyubid princes then ruled a reunified Yemen for half a century, planting Sunni Shafiʿi institutions, minting a common coinage and rebuilding the fortresses.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir; al-Maqrizi; G. Rex Smith, 'The Ayyubids and Early Rasulids in the Yemen' (1974–78).

nodes.label: The Rasulids declare a sultanate
nodes.full: When the Ayyubids left, their governor ʿUmar ibn ʿAli ibn Rasul kept Yemen for himself as al-Malik al-Mansur, founding a dynasty of Turkoman origin that claimed Ghassanid Arab descent. It ruled a unified, prosperous Yemen for 225 years.
nodes.src: al-Khazraji, al-ʿUqud al-luʾluʾiyya (the Rasulid dynastic chronicle); G. Rex Smith (1974–78).

nodes.label: Al-Malik al-Muzaffar Yusuf
nodes.full: Al-Muzaffar's forty-six-year reign was the Rasulid peak: authority extended over Hadramawt and Dhofar, the great Taʿizz madrasas built, the Aden customs organised, and a court that corresponded with Cairo, Delhi and beyond.
nodes.src: al-Khazraji; Éric Vallet, 'L'Arabie marchande: État et commerce sous les sultans rasulides du Yémen' (2010).

nodes.label: Al-Ashraf ʿUmar and the scholar-sultans
nodes.full: Al-Ashraf ʿUmar reigned barely a year but wrote on astronomy, the astrolabe, agriculture, medicine and genealogy, and several Rasulid sultans did likewise. The dynasty ran its court as a scholarly enterprise, compiling manuals of everything it governed.
nodes.src: al-Ashraf ʿUmar's works (edited by Varisco and others); Daniel Martin Varisco, 'Medieval Agriculture and Islamic Science' (1994).

nodes.label: Rasulid decline and collapse
nodes.full: Repeated plague, disputed successions, a slave-soldier faction out of control, and tribal revolt in the highlands wore the dynasty down. The last Rasulids held only fragments before the Tahirids took the south in 1454.
nodes.src: al-Khazraji; Ibn al-Dayba', Bughyat al-mustafid; Vallet (2010).

nodes.label: The Tahirids of Radaʿ
nodes.full: The Banu Tahir, local lords of Radaʿ, succeeded the Rasulids in the south and were prolific builders — the ʿAmiriyya madrasa is theirs — but weaker: pressed by the Zaydi imams in the north and by the collapse of the old Indian Ocean spice economy.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Dayba', Qurrat al-ʿuyun; Venetia Porter, 'The art and architecture of the Tahirids'.

nodes.label: The Mamluk expedition and the Ottoman handoff
nodes.full: An Egyptian Mamluk fleet sent to fight the Portuguese seized Zabid and Sanaa and killed the last Tahirid sultan. Weeks later the Ottomans conquered Egypt itself, and the stranded Mamluk force in Yemen became the nucleus of the first Ottoman garrison.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Dayba'; al-Nahrawali, al-Barq al-Yamani; Clive Smith and R. B. Serjeant on the Mamluk–Ottoman transition.

nodes.label: Al-Aswad al-ʿAnsi and the Ridda
nodes.full: The 'veiled prophet' al-Aswad al-ʿAnsi rallied Yemeni tribes against Medina and held Sanaa for months before being assassinated. The wider Ridda then had to be put down before Yemen was firmly inside the new state.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, History I; al-Waqidi, Kitab al-Ridda.

nodes.label: The Sulayhid–Najahid war
nodes.full: The Najahids killed ʿAli al-Sulayhi in 1066 and paraded his head; Queen Arwa spent decades avenging him and fighting for Zabid, and the two dynasties tore at each other across the coastal plain for a century until the Ayyubids ended both.
nodes.src: ʿUmara al-Yamani, Taʾrikh al-Yaman; Kay (1892).

nodes.label: Turan Shah reduces the highlands
nodes.full: The Ayyubid conquest was swift on the coast but slow in the mountains; it took a decade to storm or buy the highland fortresses, and the Zaydi north was never fully taken at all.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Athir; G. Rex Smith, 'The Ayyubids and Early Rasulids' (1974–78).

nodes.label: The permanent war for the highlands
nodes.full: For three centuries the Sunni sultans of the south — Ayyubid, Rasulid, Tahirid — and the Zaydi imams of the north fought over Sanaa and the central highlands. Neither side could hold the other's ground for long; the frontier simply moved back and forth.
nodes.src: al-Khazraji; the Zaydi chronicles; Vallet (2010) on the Rasulid–Zaydi wars.

nodes.label: The Rasulid–Mamluk contest over Mecca
nodes.full: The Rasulids and the Mamluks of Egypt competed for the guardianship of the Holy Cities and control of the Red Sea trade, with occasional armed clashes at Mecca during the pilgrimage. The Mamluks generally prevailed, but Yemen kept pressing.
nodes.src: al-Khazraji; al-Maqrizi; Vallet, 'L'Arabie marchande' (2010).

nodes.label: The Mamluk conquest of Zabid and Sanaa
nodes.full: The Mamluk force under Husayn al-Kurdi and then the amir Barsbay overran the Tihama and the highlands with firearms the Yemenis could not match, ending the Tahirid state — the last act of Mamluk power anywhere, weeks before Egypt fell to the Ottomans.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Dayba'; al-Nahrawali, al-Barq al-Yamani fi'l-fath al-ʿUthmani.

nodes.label: Al-Hadi's code and the Hadawi school
nodes.full: Al-Hadi wrote the law as he founded the state: his Kitab al-Ahkam and related works are the basis of the Hadawi school of Zaydi fiqh, which still governs personal status and much else in the northern highlands.
nodes.src: al-Hadi, Kitab al-Ahkam fi'l-halal wa'l-haram; Bernard Haykel, 'Revival and Reform in Islam' (2003) on the Hadawi tradition.

nodes.label: The Tayyibi daʿwa and the daʿi al-mutlaq
nodes.full: When the Fatimid line split in 1130, Queen Arwa recognised the infant Tayyib and established Yemen as the seat of the Tayyibi Ismaili mission, headed by an 'absolute missionary'. That office, later carried to India, still leads the Bohra communities.
nodes.src: the Tayyibi daʿwa histories; Daftary, 'The Ismailis' (2007); Ismail Poonawala on the daʿi al-mutlaq.

nodes.label: The Aden customs house and the Rasulid diwan
nodes.full: The Rasulids ran Aden as a fiscal machine: a published tariff on every class of goods, resident agents, a bonded warehouse, and a treasury that depended on the customs yield. The surviving registers list ships, cargoes and duties in detail.
nodes.src: the Rasulid administrative texts (Nur al-maʿarif, Irtifaʿ al-dawla); Vallet, 'L'Arabie marchande' (2010).

nodes.label: Nur al-maʿarif and Rasulid administrative science
nodes.full: The Rasulid state manuals — above all Nur al-maʿarif, 'the light of knowledge' — record tax yields, market prices, court ceremonial, trade goods, gift lists and agricultural calendars in a way almost nothing else in the medieval Islamic world does.
nodes.src: Nur al-maʿarif, ed. Muhammad ʿAbd al-Rahim Jazm (2003–05); Varisco and Vallet on the Rasulid archive.

nodes.label: Rasulid agricultural administration
nodes.full: The Rasulid sultans sponsored irrigation works, tracked the introduction of new crops in their own farming manuals, and taxed the terraced highlands and the coastal plain on a documented schedule. Agriculture was treated as a branch of statecraft.
nodes.src: al-Malik al-Afdal al-ʿAbbas, Bughyat al-fallahin; Varisco, 'Medieval Agriculture and Islamic Science' (1994).

nodes.label: The Zaydi–Hadawi tradition
nodes.full: Zaydism combined a rationalist, Muʿtazili-influenced theology with an activist doctrine of the imamate and its own school of law. Centred on Saʿda, it became the religion of the northern highland tribes and the ideology of their state.
nodes.src: van Arendonk (1960); Haykel, 'Revival and Reform in Islam' (2003); the Zaydi manuscript tradition.

nodes.label: Yemen, the last home of the Tayyibi daʿwa
nodes.full: Ismailism came to Yemen as Fatimid missionary work; after Cairo abandoned the Tayyibi line in 1130, Yemen kept it alive, elaborating an esoteric cosmology in secret. The daʿwa's leadership shifted to Gujarat only in the 16th century.
nodes.src: Daftary, 'The Ismailis' (2007); Ismail Poonawala; the Tayyibi haqaʾiq literature.

nodes.label: Shafiʿism and the madrasa in the south
nodes.full: The Ayyubids brought the Sunni Shafiʿi madrasa, and the Rasulids endowed it lavishly. The Tihama and the lower southern highlands became — and remain — solidly Shafiʿi, a religious counterweight to the Zaydi north.
nodes.src: al-Khazraji; ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Ahdal's biographical works on Zabid's scholars; R. B. Serjeant, 'The Islamic city' on Zabid.

nodes.label: Yemeni Sufism
nodes.full: Saints like Ahmad ibn ʿAlwan of Yafrus and Abu'l-Ghayth ibn Jamil drew mass followings; the Tihama grew a dense network of Sufi lodges. Sufism was the devotional life of ordinary Yemenis under every dynasty and every school.
nodes.src: al-Sharji, Tabaqat al-khawass (lives of Yemeni saints); Alexander Knysh on Ibn ʿAlwan.

nodes.label: The Hadrami sada and the ʿAlawi way
nodes.full: The descendants of Ahmad al-Muhajir, who moved to Hadramawt around 950, built at Tarim a distinctive fusion of Shafiʿi law and Sufi practice — the tariqa ʿAlawiyya — whose scholar-missionaries later carried Islam across the Indian Ocean.
nodes.src: Engseng Ho, 'The Graves of Tarim' (2006); the Hadrami biographical dictionaries (al-Shilli, al-Mashhur).

nodes.label: The Jews of Yemen and the Epistle to Yemen
nodes.full: A large, ancient Jewish community faced a messianic upheaval and a forced-conversion threat under a local ruler in the 1160s; the Yemenis wrote to Maimonides in Egypt, whose 'Epistle to Yemen' urged endurance and became a classic of the community.
nodes.src: Maimonides, Iggeret Teiman (Epistle to Yemen); S. D. Goitein on the Yemenite Jews in the Cairo Geniza.

nodes.label: The Great Mosque of Sanaa
nodes.full: One of the oldest mosques still in use, its hypostyle prayer halls set with painted coffered ceilings and columns reused from Himyarite and Christian buildings. A sealed loft in its roof held the parchment cache that yielded the Sanaa Qurʾan palimpsests.
nodes.src: Barbara Finster on the Great Mosque; von Bothmer on the manuscript find of 1972.

nodes.label: Zabid, the brick city of learning
nodes.full: Zabid is built entirely of fired brick and carved gypsum — some eighty-six historic mosques and madrasas, and a maze of decorated courtyard houses. It was one of the Arab world's great teaching towns and is now a UNESCO World Heritage site.
nodes.src: the Zabid UNESCO nomination file; Edward Keall's Canadian Archaeological Mission at Zabid.

nodes.label: Queen Arwa's Jibla
nodes.full: Arwa moved the capital from Sanaa to the small mountain town of Jibla and built its congregational mosque, converting her own palace into it. She is buried inside — one of the very few Sulayhid monuments to survive.
nodes.src: ʿUmara al-Yamani; the Jibla mosque, still standing and venerated.

nodes.label: The Rasulid madrasas of Taʿizz
nodes.full: The Ashrafiyya, Muzaffariyya and Muʿtabiyya madrasas of Taʿizz — domed, twin-minaretted, their interiors dense with carved and painted stucco — define the Rasulid architectural style and remain the city's landmarks.
nodes.src: Barbara Finster and Sabine Noja on the Taʿizz madrasas; the Rasulid architecture surveys.

nodes.label: The ʿAmiriyya of Radaʿ
nodes.full: The Tahirid madrasa at Radaʿ — five domes over a raised prayer hall, its ceilings and walls covered in painted arabesque — is among the finest and best-preserved buildings of late-medieval Arabia, restored by Selma al-Radi's long conservation project.
nodes.src: Selma al-Radi, 'The ʿAmiriya in Radaʿ: the History and Restoration of a Sixteenth-Century Madrasa in the Yemen' (1997).

nodes.label: Rasulid brass and the book
nodes.full: Inlaid brass basins and candlesticks bearing the Rasulid five-petalled rosette blazon — mostly commissioned from Mamluk Cairo — and the illuminated Qurʾans and scientific manuscripts of the Taʿizz court are the movable art of the dynasty.
nodes.src: Venetia Porter on Rasulid metalwork and the rosette blazon; the Rasulid manuscripts in the Ambrosiana and elsewhere.

nodes.label: The humayni song and the Yemeni lute
nodes.full: A colloquial sung poetry, the humayni, developed alongside the classical qasida from the Rasulid period, set to the small Yemeni lute (the qanbus or turbi). It is the root of the Sanʿani song still performed today.
nodes.src: Muhammad ʿAbduh Ghanim, 'Shiʿr al-ghinaʾ al-Sanʿani'; Jean Lambert, 'La médecine de l'âme: le chant de Sanaa' (1997).

nodes.label: The Sanaa Qurʾan palimpsest
nodes.full: Among the parchments from the Great Mosque are leaves whose visible Qurʾanic text overlies an erased earlier one — one of the very oldest Qurʾan manuscripts, and a key document in the modern study of how the text was fixed.
nodes.src: Behnam Sadeghi and Mohsen Goudarzi, 'Sanaa 1 and the origins of the Qurʾan', Der Islam (2012); Asma Hilali's edition.

nodes.label: Al-Hamdani, the tongue of Yemen
nodes.full: Al-Hasan al-Hamdani's al-Iklil gathered the genealogy and antiquities of Himyar, and his Sifat Jazirat al-ʿArab is the fullest early geography of the peninsula. Together they are the foundation of Yemen's sense of its own deep past.
nodes.src: al-Hamdani, al-Iklil (books I, II, VIII, X survive) and Sifat Jazirat al-ʿArab; D. H. Müller's and later editions.

nodes.label: Nashwan al-Himyari's Himyarite pride
nodes.full: Nashwan's great lexicon Shams al-ʿulum and his 'Himyarite ode' with its own commentary asserted a distinct, glorious South Arabian identity descended from Himyar — a counter-current to the northern-Arab genealogical mainstream.
nodes.src: Nashwan al-Himyari, Shams al-ʿulum and the Qasida al-Himyariyya; ʿAli al-Akwaʿ's editions.

nodes.label: The Rasulid learned corpus
nodes.full: The Rasulid court produced treatises on astronomy and the astrolabe, a major agronomy manual, works on medicine, veterinary science and genealogy, and a six-language word-list (the 'Rasulid Hexaglot') covering Arabic, Persian, Turkic, Greek, Armenian and Mongol.
nodes.src: Varisco, 'Medieval Agriculture and Islamic Science' (1994) and 'The Rasulid Hexaglot' (with Golden, 2000).

nodes.label: The Zaydi and Tayyibi book cultures
nodes.full: Yemen preserved two learned traditions that barely survive elsewhere: the vast Zaydi library of Saʿda — theology, hadith, law — and the secret philosophical literature of the Tayyibi daʿwa, with its Neoplatonic cosmology.
nodes.src: the Zaydi manuscript collections (Imam Zayd Cultural Foundation); Ibrahim al-Hamidi, Kanz al-walad; Daftary on the Tayyibi haqaʾiq.

nodes.label: Aden, the emporium of the Indian Ocean
nodes.full: Ships from Egypt met ships from Gujarat and Malabar at Aden, and everything transhipped there paid duty. The Cairo Geniza letters and the Rasulid registers show Aden as one of the busiest ports of the medieval world.
nodes.src: S. D. Goitein and Mordechai Friedman, 'India Traders of the Middle Ages' (2008); Vallet, 'L'Arabie marchande' (2010).

nodes.label: The Karimi merchants
nodes.full: The Karimi were the great Egypt-based wholesale houses that ran the pepper and spice trade through Aden and the Red Sea. They financed states, and their collapse in the 15th century — as the Portuguese and the Mamluks squeezed the route — helped bring down the Tahirids.
nodes.src: Walter Fischel and Subhi Labib on the Karimi; Vallet (2010).

nodes.label: The birth of coffee
nodes.full: Yemeni Sufis adopted qahwa — brewed from the roasted Ethiopian bean — as a stimulant for night devotions, and by 1500 coffee-drinking was spreading from Aden and the Yemeni highlands to Mecca and Cairo. The world's coffee habit begins here.
nodes.src: ʿAbd al-Qadir al-Jaziri, ʿUmdat al-safwa fi hill al-qahwa (c.1558), the earliest history of coffee; Ralph Hattox, 'Coffee and Coffeehouses' (1985).

nodes.label: Qat becomes a highland institution
nodes.full: The earliest datable references to chewing the leaf of Catha edulis are from Rasulid-era Yemen, where it was already a fixture of highland social and scholarly life — a stimulant crop competing with coffee for the same terraced land.
nodes.src: the Rasulid and post-Rasulid sources on qat; Shelagh Weir, 'Qat in Yemen' (1985), on its history.

nodes.label: The self-sufficient highland terrace
nodes.full: Centuries of terracing had turned the steep western highlands into a productive farmland of sorghum, wheat, grapes and, later, coffee and qat — able to feed a dense population without any dependence on the coastal trade.
nodes.src: Varisco, 'Medieval Agriculture and Islamic Science' (1994); Tony Wilkinson on Yemeni terrace systems.

nodes.label: The textiles of Zabid and the Tihama
nodes.full: Zabid and the Tihama towns wove striped and dyed cottons that were traded around the Indian Ocean and turn up by name in the Cairo Geniza. Textile manufacture was the coastal plain's main industry alongside the port trade.
nodes.src: Goitein, 'A Mediterranean Society'; R. B. Serjeant, 'Islamic Textiles: Material for a History up to the Mongol Conquest' (1972).

nodes.label: The unconquerable highland fortress
nodes.full: Fortified towns on sheer rock outcrops — Thula, Shibam Kawkaban, Zafar Dhibin, the citadel of al-Qahira above Taʿizz — could hold out for years against any besieger. This is the physical reason the Zaydi imamate could never be permanently stamped out.
nodes.src: Paolo Costa and Barbara Finster on Yemeni fortified architecture; the Rasulid and Zaydi siege narratives.

nodes.label: Cisterns and the water of the towns
nodes.full: Aden's great chain of rock-cut tanks (the Tawila cisterns) caught the rare rains that fell on the crater; highland towns cut cisterns into the jabals; Zabid and Taʿizz built aqueducts. Storing water was the precondition of every Yemeni city.
nodes.src: the Tawila Tanks of Aden; R. B. Lewcock, 'The Old Walled City of Sanaʿa' (1986) on urban water systems.

nodes.label: Brick, gypsum and carved plaster
nodes.full: The Tihama's building tradition — fired brick laid in decorative bond, finished with deeply carved white gypsum (qudad) — spread inland under the Rasulids and gave Yemeni architecture its distinctive white tracery.
nodes.src: Keall's Zabid excavations; Trevor Marchand, 'Minaret Building and Apprenticeship in Yemen' (2001) on the crafts.

nodes.label: Yemen and the Fatimid Caliphate
nodes.full: The Sulayhids ruled as Fatimid vassals and the daʿwa tied Yemen to Cairo. After the 1130 schism the relationship reversed: when the Fatimid state fell in 1171, Yemen was already the guardian of the Tayyibi branch it had backed.
nodes.src: Daftary, 'The Ismailis' (2007); Leila al-Imad on Fatimid–Sulayhid relations.

nodes.label: The Ayyubid and Mamluk connection
nodes.full: Yemen entered the Ayyubid realm by conquest, then spent two centuries as the Mamluks' southern rival — competing over Mecca, the Red Sea customs and the title of protector of the Holy Cities, and sending the kiswa and relief grain to make the claim stick.
nodes.src: al-Khazraji; al-Maqrizi; Vallet, 'L'Arabie marchande' (2010) on Rasulid–Mamluk rivalry.

nodes.label: Aden's reach to India and China
nodes.full: Rasulid Aden traded directly with Gujarat and Malabar and exchanged embassies eastward: a Rasulid mission reached the Yuan court, and the Ming treasure fleets under Zheng He called at Aden in 1419 and 1432.
nodes.src: the Rasulid sources on eastern embassies; the Ming shi-lu and Ma Huan's Ying-yai Sheng-lan on Zheng He at Aden.

nodes.label: The Hadrami diaspora begins
nodes.full: From the medieval centuries the sada and merchants of Hadramawt began settling along the Swahili coast and toward western India — scholars, judges and traders whose networks would later reach Southeast Asia and become a world diaspora.
nodes.src: Engseng Ho, 'The Graves of Tarim' (2006); the Hadrami biographical dictionaries.

nodes.label: The Portuguese break into the Indian Ocean
nodes.full: Vasco da Gama's route round Africa let Portugal contest the spice trade at its source. A failed Portuguese assault on Aden in 1513 and a blockade of the Red Sea mouth wrecked the old Karimi economy — and prompted the Mamluk fleet that ended the Tahirids.
nodes.src: the Portuguese chronicles (Barros, Correia); Serjeant, 'The Portuguese off the South Arabian Coast' (1963).

nodes.label: A country of many states
nodes.full: For most of these nine centuries Yemen held two or three polities at once — a Zaydi highland north, a Sunni south, a Tihama coast, sometimes a separate Aden or Hadramawt. The pattern set in the medieval period has never fully gone away.
nodes.src: the synthesis in Robert Burrowes and Paul Dresch, 'A History of Modern Yemen' (2000), on the deep structure; Vallet (2010).

nodes.label: The Rasulid high tide
nodes.full: For a century Yemen was unified, rich on the Aden customs, studded with madrasas, and in contact with Cairo, Delhi and China. It was the most successful and outward-facing state pre-modern Yemen ever produced.
nodes.src: Vallet, 'L'Arabie marchande' (2010); Varisco on the Rasulid intellectual project.

nodes.label: The thread continues — the Ottoman century
nodes.full: The Mamluk troops who took Zabid in 1516 were absorbed by the Ottomans, who conquered Egypt in 1517 and with it inherited a claim to Yemen. The first Ottoman occupation, the Qasimid resistance and the coffee boom are the next folio.
nodes.src: a forward reference: yemen-1517-1900 (the two Ottoman occupations, the Qasimid state and Mocha coffee) is planned but not yet built.

nodes.label: Queen Arwa bint Ahmad
nodes.full: Arwa held sovereign power in Yemen for over half a century — coins and the Friday sermon in her name, the Fatimid rank of hujja, control of the Tayyibi succession. Later Yemenis called her 'the little Queen of Sheba'; she is a touchstone for women's rule in Islamic history.
nodes.src: ʿUmara al-Yamani, Taʾrikh al-Yaman; Leila al-Imad, 'al-Sayyida al-Hurra'; Fatima Mernissi, 'The Forgotten Queens of Islam' (1993).

nodes.label: Asmaʾ bint Shihab and the Sulayhid women
nodes.full: Arwa's mother-in-law Asmaʾ bint Shihab sat unveiled in the council of state and had the khutba pronounced in her name during her husband's reign — an open, acknowledged political role for a woman that Arwa then extended into full sovereignty.
nodes.src: ʿUmara al-Yamani; al-Imad on the Sulayhid queens.

nodes.label: The slave-soldiers who became kings
nodes.full: The Najahid dynasty of Zabid was founded by two Ethiopian military slaves who seized power on their master's death. African slave-soldiers were a standing element of Tihama armies throughout the period, and the Red Sea slave trade ran both ways.
nodes.src: ʿUmara al-Yamani; Kay (1892); Éric Vallet on the Rasulid slave troops.

nodes.label: The Jews of Yemen
nodes.full: An ancient community, mostly craftsmen and silversmiths, living under the dhimma across every dynasty and periodically squeezed — the 1160s messianic crisis, later expulsions from the north. They sustained a distinctive liturgy and a rich tradition of Hebrew poetry.
nodes.src: Goitein on the Yemenite Jews; Yosef Tobi, 'The Jews of Yemen' (1999).
